MESSAGE:
Need a hand with our quarterly marketing report, it's due Friday and I'm behind.

First, give me a better title than "Q3 Marketing Report", ideally something that signals it's about what actually worked. Second, what chart type would you use to show monthly signups across three channels over the quarter? Also define "bounce rate" in one line for the execs, and suggest three questions they're likely to ask so I can prep answers.

Landing page A got 2,000 visits and converted at 10%. Landing page B got 200 visits and converted at 30%. In the summary slide I was going to write "overall conversion rate across both pages was 20%". Is that the right figure to report? If not, what is it?

Should the detailed appendix tables go at the back of the slide deck or in a separate spreadsheet that I link to? Our CFO likes to dig into numbers but the CEO hates long decks, so I'm a bit torn on that one. Whatever you suggest, I'll need to defend it in the meeting.

Thanks, you're a lifesaver. I'll be working through all of these tonight and tomorrow morning.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a better report title
2. Recommend a chart type for monthly signups across three channels
3. Define 'bounce rate' in one line
4. Suggest three likely exec questions
5. Check the 20% overall conversion figure and give the correct one  KEY: 20% is wrong (it is an unweighted average of two rates). Pooled rate = (200 + 60) / (2,000 + 200) = 260 / 2,200 = about 11.8%. Must report ~11.8%.
6. Recommend appendix tables in the deck vs a separate spreadsheet

ANSWER:
## Overall conversion rate: **11.8%, not 20%**

20% is the average of the two rates, but the pages had very different traffic, so a simple average misleads. Count the conversions instead:

| Page | Visits | Rate | Conversions |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2,000 | 10% | 200 |
| B | 200 | 30% | 60 |
| **Total** | **2,200** | | **260** |

260 ÷ 2,200 = **11.8%**. Most of the traffic went to page A, so the overall rate sits close to A's 10%.

The execs will probably ask whether you should send all traffic to page B. Prep for it.
- **The gap looks real.** Even with only 200 visits, B's rate sits well above A's.
- **But it may not be the page.** If B's visitors came from a different source or campaign, they may simply have been more ready to buy.
- **A safe answer:** "B looks promising. We'll test it by splitting the same traffic between both pages next quarter."

## Title

Something that leads with the takeaway:

> **Q3 Marketing: What Drove Growth, and Where We'll Invest Next**

Or, once you know your headline finding, make it specific: "**Q3 Marketing: [Channel] Led Signup Growth; [Page B] Points to Higher Conversion**".

## Chart for monthly signups by channel

A **clustered column chart**: the three months along the bottom, with three bars per month, one for each channel. With only three data points per channel, columns are easier to read than lines. If the total also matters, use a **stacked column** instead, so each bar shows the month's total split by channel.

## Bounce rate, in one line

> The percentage of visitors who leave after viewing a single page without interacting further.

If your numbers come from Google Analytics 4, it defines bounce rate as the share of sessions that weren't "engaged" (for example, under 10 seconds with no further action). Check which definition your figures use in case someone asks.

## Three questions to prep for

1. **What did each channel cost per signup, and which gives the best return?** Have cost per acquisition by channel ready.
2. **How does this compare with last quarter and with our targets?** Have the quarter-on-quarter change and the gap to target for the headline numbers.
3. **What are we changing in Q4 based on this?** For example, testing page B more widely, or shifting budget toward the best-performing channel.

## Appendix: back of the deck or a separate spreadsheet?

**Use a linked spreadsheet for the detailed tables, plus two or three backup slides at the end of the deck.**

How to defend it:
- **The CEO gets a short deck.** The main story stays tight, and the backup slides sit after the end and only come up if needed.
- **The CFO gets more than slides could give.** A spreadsheet can be sorted, filtered and checked, which is what someone who digs into numbers actually wants.
- **The backup slides cover live questions.** They hold the handful of figures you expect to be asked about in the meeting, such as cost per signup by channel, so you won't need to open the spreadsheet mid-meeting.

A one-line defence: "The deck tells the story; the spreadsheet holds every number, so nobody has to choose between a short meeting and full detail."

Good luck with Friday!
